title: Fair pay
tomorrow: the set's headed for a dumpster. why does a war law stop for trees?

cards: Why sundown? Because the Torah says the hired worker is poor, "and setteth his heart upon it." Tonight's groceries ride on today's pay.
The Talmud tells a story that pushes further. Porters are hauling barrels of wine for a rabbi named Rabbah bar bar Hana, and they drop them. The barrels split, and the wine soaks into the dirt.
He's furious, and he takes their cloaks to cover the loss. The porters go to Rav, the town's great teacher. Whose side will he take?

teach.b: Rav says: give them back their cloaks. Is that the law? Rabbah asks.
Rav answers with a line from Proverbs: so that you walk in the way of good people. The cloaks go back.
Then the porters speak up: we're poor, we worked all day, we're hungry, and we have nothing. Rav says: pay them. Is that the law?
Yes, says Rav, and finishes the verse: and keep the paths of the righteous. Look at what just happened. By the letter of the law, the porters might owe for the wine.

teach.h: PAST THE LETTER OF THE LAW.
teach.b: Rav reaches past the letter, toward what the verse calls good and righteous, because a day's pay is a day's food. The Torah's own rule is plain.
Don't hold back a hired worker's wages; pay them the same day, before the sun goes down. Leviticus adds that the wages shouldn't stay with you all night until morning.
Lived today, pay today looks like the sitter paid at the door, not later; a freelancer's invoice paid when it arrives; the kid who shoveled your walk paid before the snow melts.
Something to tell a friend tonight: in this Talmud story, a rabbi tells an employer to pay the workers who broke his barrels.

how: Jewish law treats paying a worker on time as a commandment; many observant employers and families make a point of paying sitters, cleaners and day workers the same day the work is done.

a fee charged for being paid in cash
paying workers fully and on time, the same day

when a day's wages are due

s: in the story, Rav lets the employer keep the cloaks to cover the wine
Rav tells him to give the cloaks back, and then to pay the porters too.
the Torah says to pay a hired worker the same day
'neither shall the sun go down upon it; for he is poor, and setteth his heart upon it.'
paying on time only matters for big employers
the verse is about any hired worker: a sitter, a neighbor's kid, a freelancer.

games.q: you hired a neighbor's kid to rake leaves. she finishes at five, and you've only got a big bill, no change. what fits pay today?
o: find a way to pay her tonight, even if it means a trip for change.
pay her next time you see her; it's only a small amount.
round it down to what you have in coins; she'll understand.
games.why: the wage is due before sundown because the worker has set her heart on it. small amounts count too.

practice: Run through the people you owe, even small amounts: a friend who covered lunch, a sitter, a neighbor's kid who raked the leaves. Pick one.
With your next few slow breaths, settle it if you can, or set the exact hour today when you will.

wordCard.voice: Fair pay: paying workers fully and promptly, before sundown, because they've set their heart on it.

carryVoice: The line to keep: pay today, before the sun goes down on anyone's wages. Eight days in.
